anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statements or transaction patterns that unnecessarily scan, join, or retain more data or longer transactions than the business logic requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records that outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and visibility-check costs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Mis-tuned engine parameters governing memory, background workers, checkpoints, and parallelism that are misaligned with workload characteristics and hardware capacity.

When all three conditions coincide, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: 1) a growing population of slow and timing-out queries whose latency is dominated by both excessive data access and ever-larger version chains; 2) rapid bloat of tables, indexes, and version stores causing drastic drops in cache hit ratios and longer sequential scans; 3) cleanup workers and checkpoints alternately starving or overrunning I/O, leading to bursty disk activity, checkpoint storms, and erratic throughput; 4) inflated lock and snapshot lifetimes that cascade into higher memory footprint and transaction-ID wraparound warnings; 5) monitoring views show paradoxical resource utilization—CPU under-utilized during I/O stalls, or vice versa—because mis-set parameters throttle some subsystems while others are saturated.

Causally, chatty or long-lived application transactions (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly) generate large volumes of updates and deletes, creating an abundant supply of dead tuples. MVCC cleanup must work harder, but its effectiveness is hampered both by the lingering snapshots held open by those same long transactions and by conservative maintenance thresholds or memory/I/O caps imposed by sub-optimal configuration parameters. As version bloat increases, query plans degrade and force even wider scans, further amplifying the workload logic inefficiency. Simultaneously, poorly sized buffer pools, work memories, and checkpoint intervals intensify I/O pressure, slowing both user queries and vacuum/garbage-collection workers. The feedback loop of bloated storage, sluggish cleanup, and ever-costlier queries drives the system into chronic performance instability, particularly under high-concurrency OLTP conditions.

entry.official_description: The file '%-.128s' must be in the database directory or be readable by all
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
